title: Looking at Classical Education
author: Albert Cheng and Helen Baxendale
summary: Albert Cheng and Helen Baxendale introduce the Empeiria File, a new ON Classical Education section devoted to empirical research, and argue that classical educators should welcome rather than fear evidence about their claims. They begin from Brian Polk's challenge that if the movement claims to form the whole person and cultivate virtue, it must ask honestly whether it actually does so, noting that this is an empirical question. Acknowledging classical skepticism of empiricism, which descends from Bacon's rejection of Aristotle, they turn to C.S. Lewis's 'Meditation in a Toolshed' distinction between 'looking along' an experience and 'looking at' it, insisting both are needed and each can correct the other. They give three uses of research: vindicating practices like explicit phonics and memorization, adding empirical ballast to normatively justified practices like handwriting, and informing contested choices such as math instruction styles and mixed-ability grouping. They concede research tells what is rather than what ought to be, and close with oenologist Émile Peynaud's line that 'tradition is an experiment that worked.'
points: Polk's challenge frames classical education's big claims about forming virtue and flourishing as empirical questions that deserve honest testing.
Lewis's 'looking along' versus 'looking at' distinction lets the authors defend empirical study without surrendering the lived, normative knowledge of teachers.
Science of reading research vindicates phonics, read-alouds, and memorization that classical schools used while mainstream schools and education departments rejected them.
Evidence that mixed-ability math classes slow the most able without lifting the weakest poses a real tradeoff for classical schools' communal commitments.
The Empeiria File promises to publish unflattering findings as well as supportive ones, positioning evidence as a prompt for self-correction.
quotes: Those are beautiful and significant claims. And if we’re going to make them, we ought to be willing to ask an honest question: Is it true, are we really doing it?

But the question about the efficacy of classical education is an empirical one. And answers to empirical questions can be informed by empirical research. And as Clare Basil and Daniel Buck have observed, the empirical research tradition has not, to date, played a significant role in answering questions about classical education or informing the practice of teaching, learning, and leadership in classical schools. In fact, there is some skepticism of the empirical research tradition in classical schools.

Rather, Lewis points out that one must always both look along and at things, and because of that inevitably, he admonishes us to do the hard work of discerning if each way of seeing helps us see what is true. Sometimes, looking at might lead us to the wrong conclusions. Other times, looking along leads to self-deception. Still other times, both ways of seeing may be invalid or incomplete. Or perhaps both shed light on the truth in different ways, enabling us to see more clearly.

Teachers and leaders already spend a lot of time looking along. They experience head on the life of a school, interact constantly with students, and make innumerable everyday observations—all of which yield insight in the pursuit of excellence in their work. But looking along classical education is enhanced by the scientific work of looking at classical education.

Looking at can provide additional empirical ballast for practices classical educators have embraced primarily for normative reasons particular to the classical approach. For example, classical educators often make students practice handwriting and learn cursive mostly because cursive is beautiful and serves the aim of shaping students’ aesthetic tastes. That alone is sufficient justification, but evidence is accumulating that handwriting is beneficial to cognitive development.

But Peynaud countered that these old, revered cellar practices weren’t handed down by magic; they were themselves - at least originally - empirical, functional solutions discovered through trial and error. Therefore, modern, scientific approaches shouldn’t be derided or feared as enemies of heritage, but embraced as a continuation (and in some cases, a powerful validation) of the exact same rational testing process that created the traditions in the first place. As Peynaud pithily put it: “Tradition is an experiment that worked.

But that would be a mistake. Just like viticulture and viniculture, much of what comprises the bedrock of classical education might rightly be considered an experiment—in pedagogy, form, and content—that *worked* and so passed into tradition.
